target_customer: iPad and iPhone users who paint and sketch, from hobbyists to professional artists
problem: Touch screens had no good native painting tool in 2009 and 2010. Brushes offered layered painting with replayable strokes for a few dollars.
business_model: paid app (about 3 dollars per the sources); later free and open source

founders.name: Steve Sprang
founders.background_notes: Credited as creator of Brushes for iPhone in 2009 and iPad in 2010 on the App Store listing. Education not found.

founders.name: Kurt Revis
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page only.

exit.reason: Brushes 3 was removed from the App Store in 2015 per the app listing; the source code was later released as open source and a different developer (Envoza) now publishes Brushes 4

competitors.name: Sketchbook Pro
competitors.what: Autodesk iPad sketching and painting app, praised for line quality and layers
competitors.traction_then: Engadget named it its iPad winner for basic drawing and painting in April 2010

competitors.name: Adobe Ideas
competitors.what: Simple vector sketch app from Adobe

technical_complexity.rationale: Smooth stroke rendering, layers and stroke replay on early iPad hardware needed solid graphics work, but the app was built by essentially one developer.

defensibility.rationale: Reviewers favored Sketchbook Pro on features, and rivals on a closed app store platform shipped alike. Prestige users like Hockney gave it reputation, not lock in.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Neither acquired it. Brushes 3 was pulled from the App Store in 2015, and the author later open sourced Brushes and Inkpad.

market_need_then: The iPad launched in April 2010 and creative apps were a showcase category. Artists such as David Hockney and illustrator Jorge Colombo (New Yorker cover, June 2009) used Brushes.

branding.domain_note: Used brushesapp.com (app suffix), which now announces the open source release.
branding.brand_signature: Use by David Hockney and the June 2009 New Yorker cover drawn on an iPhone with Brushes
branding.community_and_virality: A companion Brushes Viewer replayed paintings stroke by stroke, a community gallery existed, and press covered Hockney and the New Yorker cover.

brand_strength.rationale: Prestige artist use and magazine press gave strong credibility among artists, but the name is generic and no source shows it driving mass growth.

outcome_analysis: Brushes gained credibility through use by David Hockney and a New Yorker cover, but reviewers in 2010 preferred Sketchbook Pro on features and the product stayed a one developer app. Brushes 3 left the App Store in 2015, a community fork said the author was unreachable from March 2014, and the code was later open sourced. The YC listing says inactive; no funding or commercial figures were found, and the stated cause of decline is not public.
notes: No funding information found in a funding search or in a Crunchbase/Wikipedia cross-check (the vcbacked page had no data). Exit type is unknown: the app lived on under other publishers, so this is not clearly a shutdown. The brand sources came from search results and were not opened; the Hockney and New Yorker items are from outlets dated 2009 and 2010. The YC page does not list founder bios.
